paras: The threatened Klan attack on Black residents of Birmingham was a planned massacre and expulsion of the Black population of Birmingham, Alabama, that the writer William Pickens said was set for a Saturday night in March 1919. According to Pickens, the attack was called off because Black residents were armed and ready to defend themselves, and no one was reported hurt. The Plaindealer printed his account under the headline "ARMED BLACKS AVERT HORRIBLE MASSACRE" as an example of courage averting a second East St. Louis.

Pickens traced the plan to white resentment of Black soldiers returning from Europe, whose bearing on the streets "seemed to demand respect." Notices of the Ku Klux Klan, styled "The Invisible Empire," appeared daily in the papers, and white children began to taunt returned Black soldiers. When a Black speaker called for the ballot and mixed juries, the Birmingham News published a letter describing the Klan as "not an anti Negro organization" but one that stood for "the supremacy of the white race."

On the appointed Saturday, white families dismissed their Black servants early, warning of "trouble," but Pickens reported that no Black resident left town. White men formed waiting lines at gun stores and displayed their new rifles and revolvers, while police disarmed and arrested Black men found carrying guns. That night Black men stayed on the streets, and several riot calls came in from different parts of the city, but only the police responded. One policeman, a former member of the Foreign Legion, was said to have advised whites not to attack.
The massacre, in Pickens's words, was "indefinitely postponed"; afterward a "Joint Committee on Race Relations" of white and Black members was organized, and the Klan's proclamations stopped.

The account appeared on the front page of the Plaindealer on May 9, 1919, as a signed article by Pickens, who said he told the story "for those who dare not tell it." Pickens framed it as a lesson in Black self-defense, offered some details as hearsay, and closed by calling the Klan "a clannish, secret, cowardly organization of midnight bullies and assasins." No other Black-press account of the planned attack appears in the coverage; Seattle's Cayton's Weekly mentioned only that Klan demonstrations had occurred at Birmingham among other Alabama towns.

reader.title: Threatened Klan attack on Black residents of Birmingham (1919)
bases: Pickens describes a Klan propaganda campaign and a planned Saturday-night massacre and expulsion that was threatened but did not take place, with no one reported killed or injured (A2, A3, A5).

The whole account is one article by William Pickens split into four fragments (A2-A5); Cayton's Weekly mentions Klan demonstrations at Birmingham only in passing and does not describe the planned attack (A6).

accounts.label: Black correspondent (William Pickens)
accounts.gist: A Klan-led campaign set a Saturday night in March 1919 to drive Black people from Birmingham; Black residents' armed and disciplined readiness caused the attack to be called off.

accounts.label: Cayton's Weekly editorial
accounts.gist: Lists Birmingham among Alabama towns where the revived Klan has held demonstrations aimed at terrorizing returning Black soldiers.

framing.detail: Headlined 'ARMED BLACKS AVERT HORRIBLE MASSACRE', Pickens's article calls the Klan 'a clannish, secret, cowardly organization of midnight bullies and assasins' and credits 'the courage of the Birmingham Negro'.
Cayton's Weekly treats the Klan's Alabama demonstrations as an effort to terrorize returning Black soldiers 'into servility and subservience'.

sources.note: Pleasanton, Kansas social column; segmentation attached the headline of the Pickens article ('ARMED BLACKS AVERT HORRIBLE MASSACRE') to its end; cited only for that headline.
William Pickens, part 1: a massacre and expulsion scheduled for a March 1919 week-end in Birmingham; returned Black soldiers resented; Klan notices in the papers.
quotes: a great massacre and expulsion of colored people was scheduled to take place in Birmingham, Aia, at one week-end of March, 1919
"We've got to teach these niggers a lesson," was the final verdict.

sources.note: Pickens, part 2: Klan proclamations, Birmingham News letter, whites tracked gun sales to Negroes, 'the day' set for a Saturday night, servants dismissed early.
quotes: White people kept a careful record of all guns sold to Negroes, and exaggerated the number, to further inflame, or to justify, the "Klan."

sources.note: Pickens, part 3: white men lined up at gun stores, police disarmed and arrested Black men, Black men stayed on the streets, riot calls answered only by police.
quotes: they cunningly disarmed every Negro they could find with a gun.
Several riot calls were turned in that night from different sections of the city, but only the police responded.

sources.note: Pickens, part 4: massacre 'indefinitely postponed'; Black defensive plans (hearsay); Joint Committee on Race Relations formed; Klan proclamations stopped.
quotes: "What good would it have done to kill 200 or 300 niggers, if 25 or 30 white men got killed?" He was conservative.

sources.note: Editorial: Klan demonstrations have occurred at Birmingham, Mobile, Troy and other Alabama towns; aimed at terrorizing returning Black soldiers; no Birmingham detail.
quotes: Other demonstrations of this Klan—resurrected after a burial of forty years—have occurred at Birmingham, Mobile, Troy and other smaller towns
